deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture notes or excerpts on ancient Egyptian history, continuing the 'Erste Periode der Geschichte' (from the earliest times to Psammetich's sole rule, 660 BC) begun on the previous page. Content: (1) Egypt already appears as a civilized people and probably a kingdom at an early date, though it is unknown whether it covered all of Egypt. (2) Kings held great power, but priests stood beside them and had to be consulted. (3) There are traces of obelisks but not of pyramids. (4) A partly illegible remark: an unclear term (transcribed 'Hirtenstaat'), 'schien sehr gebildet', with 'aber' corrected to 'ein' before 'Handelsvolk'. (5) Castes formed very early, defined as hereditary divisions into estates. (6) Herodotus names 7 castes: priests, warriors, boatmen/pilots, interpreters, tradesmen, cowherds, swineherds. (7) Only the two capitals Thebes and Memphis are documented. Osymandias and Busiris ruled in Thebes. Menes, Moeris and the most famous, Sesostris, ruled at Memphis. (8) Sesostris was a great conqueror, said to have conquered Arabia, most of Asia and Europe. He dug canals throughout Egypt and set up 4 great colossi at the temple of Vulcan (Hephaestus/Ptah) at Memphis. (9) Towards the end of the period Sethos reigned, c. 700 BC; after his death Egypt was divided (into 12 states, continued on the next page). There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The page reads like notes from a Göttingen history lecture in the style of Heeren's ancient history, using a Herodotean chronology. The hand and subject suggest it may not be a Gauss mathematical manuscript at all, perhaps a family member's or student's notebook bound into the bundle.
errors: Historical, not mathematical: Herodotus (2.110) says Sesostris left six statues before the temple of Hephaestus (himself, his wife and four sons). Only the four sons' statues were 20 cubits; the 'two 30-cubit' figures belong to himself and his wife, so '4 große Kolossen' is a simplification.
Sesostris's conquest of 'Europe' (Thrace/Scythia) and most of Asia is Herodotean legend; this reflects the source tradition rather than a slip by the writer.
The date 'Psammetich ... 660' is a rounded value of the period; modern chronology puts his accession at 664 BC.

results.what: Herodotus' list of seven Egyptian castes and the legendary king sequence (Menes, Moeris, Sesostris, Sethos) in a history lecture
results.modern_name: Not mathematics: lecture notes on ancient Egyptian history (Herodotus, Histories II)
results.usually_credited_to: Herodotus; German Göttingen ancient-history lecture tradition (e.g. A. H. L. Heeren)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is purely historical school or lecture material on ancient Egypt with no mathematical content. It is entirely routine and likely not even Gauss's own work.

checkable.asserts: Length in years of the 'second period' (Psammetich's sole rule to Cambyses' conquest) as dated in the notes on the next page
With a modern accession date of 664 BC and the stated 54-year reign, Psammetich dies in 610 BC, consistent with Necho II's accession

transcription_corrections: 'Gegen Ende dieses Periode' should read 'Gegen Ende dieser Periode'.
'Er[?] soll Arabien' is plausibly 'Er soll Arabien'.
'an dem Tempel des Vulcan[?] führte er[?]' is consistent with the image and with Herodotus (temple of Hephaestus = Vulcan at Memphis).

'Der Hirtenstaat[?] schien sehr gebildet, ein Handelsvolk schon[?] der[?]' remains uncertain. The first word may be a different compound (e.g. '...stand'), and the clause appears to contrast degree of civilization with trade; the reading should stay flagged.
'Unter Kaste verstehen wir Eintheilung' likely has 'eine' before 'Eintheilung' ('verstehen wir eine Eintheilung in Stände').
